claims.text: Plastic deformation in equiatomic FCC CoCrFeNi under uniaxial tension will be governed primarily by dislocation glide on {111} planes.
Deformation twinning or transformation-induced plasticity will occur only when the stacking-fault energy is sufficiently low.
At room temperature, yield strength will be insensitive to strain rates below 10^-4 s^-1.
Room-temperature strain-rate insensitivity is caused by athermal obstacles comprising solute atoms and lattice friction.
Yield strength will exhibit significant strain-rate sensitivity above 10^-2 s^-1.
Above 0.5 Tm, thermal activation will produce significant strain-rate sensitivity by aiding dislocation cross-slip.
Above approximately 0.6 Tm, yield strength will become insensitive to strain rate because thermal activation overcomes the Peierls barrier.
Yield strength in the target alloy is controlled by interactions of dislocations with solute atoms and grain boundaries.
NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 exhibits a high-temperature strength plateau from approximately 873 K to 1073 K.
The high-temperature plateau should shift to lower temperatures in FCC CoCrFeNi than in BCC refractory alloys because FCC alloys have lower Peierls stress.
Yield strength will increase as temperature decreases.
Yield strength will increase as strain rate increases.
The target FCC alloy will exhibit a yield-strength plateau between 800 K and 1000 K.
Strain-rate sensitivity in the 800–1000 K plateau will fall below n = 0.05.
If stacking-fault energy is below 20 mJ/m^2, the deformation mechanism will shift to TRIP or TWIP.
Twin nucleation at low stacking-fault energy may increase strain-rate sensitivity.
Deformation twins formed at higher strains will increase work hardening.
Corrosion resistance is inversely correlated with deformation-induced defect density because dislocations and twins act as active sites for localized corrosion.
Standard FCC CoCrFeNi alloys typically have room-temperature yield strengths of 200–400 MPa.
Standard FCC CoCrFeNi alloys typically exhibit room-temperature ductility above 50%.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis predicts significant strain-rate sensitivity above 0.5 Tm because of thermal activation, but also places strain-rate insensitivity and n < 0.05 above roughly 0.6 Tm because thermal activation is no longer rate limiting. These overlapping temperature regimes imply opposite rate-sensitivity behavior.
